To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the degree of synergistic interactions reported for insecticidal proteins is generally low, the reported interactions are sometimes inconclusive due to unproven testing assumptions or other bioanalytical challenges, and many of the reported synergistic interactions may be artefact.

i) the majority of studies reporting synergistic interactions among insecticidal protein mixtures have been conducted using bioassay models which may not be appropriate, ii) reported interactions are low in magnitude, and iii) many interactions may not be artefactual.

i) the majority of insecticidal protein interaction data are inconclusive due to unproven assumptions, ii) the magnitude of synergism reported in the literature is low, and iii) the majority of interactions are not synergistic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interpretation of laboratory interaction data and the implications for risk assessment.
the question of whether laboratory bioassays of the type commonly used to assess insecticidal protein interactions are capable of detecting synergistic effects in the field.
the development of a framework to help guide and interpret interaction data, which can be used to support regulatory decision-making.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for the most part, the whole is not greater than the sum of its parts.
the majority of interaction studies conducted to date have been inconclusive.
there is little or no synergistic interaction among the insecticidal toxins of Bt plants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current body of literature is not sufficient to conclude that additive models are not predictive of the potential for insecticidal protein interactions.
the majority of studies reporting insecticidal protein interactions have not provided the data required for a meaningful assessment of the interaction.
while there is no doubt that synergistic interactions exist, there is a lack of data demonstrating their significance in terms of safety assessment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a bioassay method which generates a high degree of biological response variation will likely result in a high proportion of equivocal/inconclusion interactions.
the current data do not support the use of interaction testing to justify any changes to the current GM crop safety assessment paradigm.

, when the whole is not greater than the sum of the parts, a thorough understanding of the underlying bioassay assumptions and the biological mechanisms of the insecticidals are required to ensure a robust and meaningful synergy assessment.
